title: Given an unsorted array of numbers, find the K numbers that appear most frequently. Explain how a frequency map plus a min-heap keyed on frequency finds them efficiently.
shortTitle: Top K Frequent Numbers (Find the K Most Frequently Occurring Numbers)
keyPoints: First count frequencies of each number in a hash map in O(n) time.
Then maintain a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency, where the root is the least frequent of the K most frequent kept.
When the heap overflows beyond K, the least frequent number is evicted.
Time complexity is O(n + d log K) where d is the number of distinct values.
When K approaches the number of distinct values, bucket sort by frequency gives O(n) time.
This combines two patterns: frequency counting and Top K Elements with a min-heap.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies in a hash map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap overflows.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Frequency map** – a hash map counting occurrences of each number in O(n) time.
- **Min-heap keyed on frequency** – the root holds the number with the lowest frequency among the K kept, making eviction of the weakest a single poll.
- **Overflow eviction** – when the heap exceeds size K after an offer, poll removes the least frequent number.
- **O(n + d log K) time** – counting is O(n), and each of the d distinct values costs at most O(log K) for a heap operation.
- **Bucket sort alternative** – when K is close to d, a bucket sort by frequency gives O(n) time by reading buckets from the high end.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh wants to find the K merchant categories he spends on most often from a long transaction history. He first tallies how many times each category appears, then keeps a small bucket of the K most frequent categories, where the least frequent kept category sits on top so a more frequent one can push it out.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Frequent Numbers combines frequency counting with the Top K Elements pattern. You first pass over the array and count how many times each number occurs in a hash map. Then you keep a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency, where the root is the least frequent of the numbers you are currently keeping. As you iterate over the distinct numbers, each one is offered to the heap, and when the heap grows beyond K, the root (least frequent) is evicted.

The overflow-then-evict step guarantees you always discard the weakest candidate, so after processing every distinct number the heap holds exactly the K most frequent ones. The counting is O(n) and the heap work is O(d log K) where d is the number of distinct values.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to find the K merchant categories a customer transacts in most often, powering a rewards recommendation from a long transaction history. He counted category frequencies once and kept a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent kept category whenever a more frequent one arrived.

The senior-level insight is knowing when to switch tools: when K is close to the number of distinct values, a bucket sort by frequency achieves O(n) time by placing numbers in frequency-indexed buckets and reading from the high end. Mentioning both approaches shows depth.

Remember one sentence: count frequencies in a map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency to hold the K most frequent numbers.
